title.en: Model Families, Licenses and Use Cases

body.en:
The open-source LLM landscape is organized around model families — groups of models sharing an architecture, training methodology, and release lineage. Key families include Meta's Llama series (Llama 2, Llama 3), Mistral AI's Mistral and Mixtral models, the Falcon family from TII, and Google's Gemma. Each family offers multiple size variants (7B, 13B, 70B parameters) to balance performance and resource cost.

Licenses define what you can legally do with a model. Apache 2.0 and MIT licenses allow broad commercial use with minimal restrictions. The Llama Community License permits commercial use but restricts redistribution at scale. Some models use custom licenses that prohibit specific applications.

Use cases drive model selection: instruction-following models (e.g., Llama-3-Instruct, Mistral-Instruct) excel at chat and task completion; base models suit continued pre-training; code-specialized models like DeepSeek Coder or CodeLlama target software engineering tasks; embedding models like BGE or E5 power semantic search and RAG pipelines.

An embedding model like BGE-Large
An instruction-tuned chat model like Llama-3-8B-Instruct
A code-specialized model like CodeLlama

explanation.en: Instruction-tuned chat models are trained to follow prompts and engage in dialogue, making them the natural choice for a customer-facing chatbot. Base models lack instruction-following behavior, embedding models produce vectors not text, and code models are optimized for programming tasks.

question.en: The Mixtral 8x7B model belongs to which architectural category?

text.en: Dense transformer with 56B active parameters
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model activating a subset of parameters per token
Retrieval-augmented generation model with built-in search
Encoder-only model similar to BERT

explanation.en: Mixtral 8x7B uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture where only 2 out of 8 expert layers are activated per token, giving it roughly 13B active parameters during inference despite having 47B total parameters. title.en: Hugging Face Hub, Model Cards and Datasets

body.en:
The Hugging Face Hub (huggingface.co) is the central repository for the open-source ML community, hosting over 500,000 models, 150,000 datasets, and thousands of Spaces (interactive demos). It provides a git-based versioning system for model weights, tokenizer configs, and documentation.

Model Cards are structured README files that accompany every model repository. A well-written model card describes the model's intended use, training data, evaluation results, ethical considerations, and known limitations. The Hub enforces a standard schema so downstream tooling can parse key metadata automatically.

The datasets library (pip install datasets) provides a unified API to load, stream, and preprocess any dataset hosted on the Hub. Datasets are stored in Apache Arrow format for memory efficiency and support streaming for datasets too large to fit in RAM.

Hub authentication via User Access Tokens (huggingface_hub login or HF_TOKEN env variable) is required to download gated models like Llama 3 or Gemma. The huggingface_hub Python library exposes programmatic search, file upload, and repository management, enabling CI/CD integration.

question.en: What is the primary purpose of a model card on the Hugging Face Hub?

text.en: To store the model's binary weights in a compressed format
To document intended use, training data, evaluation results, limitations, and ethical considerations
To provide a live API endpoint for inference requests
To list the hardware requirements for local deployment only

explanation.en: A model card is a structured documentation artifact — not a weight file or API. Its purpose is to transparently communicate what the model is designed for, what data trained it, how it performs on benchmarks, and what its limitations and risks are, enabling informed adoption decisions.

question.en: You want to load a large dataset (500 GB) for training without downloading it entirely to disk. Which Hugging Face datasets feature should you use?

text.en: load_dataset with split='train[:100%]'
load_dataset with streaming=True
datasets.load_from_disk()
datasets.concatenate_datasets()

explanation.en: Setting streaming=True in load_dataset enables on-the-fly data fetching row by row without downloading the full dataset to disk. This is essential for very large datasets that exceed local storage or RAM capacity. The other options either require full local availability or serve different purposes.

Submitting a formal research proposal to Meta
Downloading the weights directly from Meta's GitHub repository

explanation.en: Gated models require two steps: (1) visiting the model's Hub page and accepting the license agreement with your Hugging Face account, and (2) authenticating your local environment with a User Access Token via huggingface-cli login or the HF_TOKEN environment variable. The Hugging Face transformers library is the standard interface for loading and running open-source models. The pipeline() function provides a high-level abstraction: you specify a task (e.g., 'text-generation', 'text-classification', 'summarization') and a model identifier, and the library handles model loading, tokenization, inference, and decoding automatically.

Under the hood, every pipeline runs a tokenizer before the model. Tokenizers convert raw text strings into sequences of integer token IDs that the model can process. The most common algorithms are Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE), used by GPT-family and Llama models; WordPiece, used by BERT; and SentencePiece, used by T5 and many multilingual models. All split text into subword units, balancing vocabulary size against coverage of rare words.

Special tokens are reserved IDs with structural meaning: the Beginning-of-Sequence token (BOS/CLS) marks input start; End-of-Sequence (EOS/SEP) marks the end; PAD tokens align sequences in a batch to equal length; and chat models add role-specific tokens like [INST] or <|user|>. Mishandling special tokens is a leading cause of degraded model performance when building custom inference pipelines.

question.en: Why is it important to use padding tokens when batching multiple sequences together for inference?

text.en: Padding tokens increase the model's vocabulary size dynamically
Transformer models require all sequences in a batch to have identical length; padding fills shorter sequences to match the longest
Padding tokens act as separators between different documents in a sequence
Padding is only needed for encoder-decoder models, not decoder-only LLMs

explanation.en: Transformer computations are performed on fixed-shape tensors, so all sequences in a batch must share the same token length. body.en:
Every LLM deployment starts with three strategic options. Hosted API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral AI, Cohere) offers the fastest time-to-value with no infrastructure overhead, but introduces data privacy concerns, vendor lock-in, per-token costs that scale with usage, and network latency. It is the right default for prototyping and low-volume production where data sensitivity is low.

Local model deployment (running a model on your own GPU cluster or edge hardware) eliminates API costs at scale and keeps data on-premises, satisfying strict data governance requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, financial regulation). The trade-off is infrastructure ownership, DevOps complexity, and higher upfront cost. Quantized models (GGUF via llama.cpp, GPTQ, AWQ) reduce GPU memory requirements significantly.

Fine-tuning is warranted when the base or instruction-tuned model consistently fails on your specific domain despite careful prompt engineering — for example, adapting a model to a proprietary coding style, a specialized scientific vocabulary, or a specific output schema. Techniques include full fine-tuning, LoRA/QLoRA (parameter-efficient), and instruction fine-tuning on curated task datasets. Fine-tuning adds training cost, data curation effort, and an ongoing model maintenance burden; it should be a deliberate choice, not a default.

question.en: A healthcare company needs to process patient records with an LLM to extract clinical entities. Their data is covered by HIPAA. Which deployment strategy is most appropriate?

text.en: OpenAI GPT-4 API with default settings
Local deployment of an open-source model on the company's on-premises infrastructure
A public Hugging Face Space running a shared model
A third-party API with no data processing agreement

explanation.en: HIPAA-regulated patient data must not be transmitted to third-party API endpoints without a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA) and appropriate data handling controls. Local deployment on on-premises infrastructure keeps patient data within the organization's security perimeter, satisfying regulatory requirements. Public Spaces and unagreed third-party APIs are clearly non-compliant.

question.en: You have a general-purpose Llama-3-8B-Instruct model and want it to consistently output valid JSON matching a specific schema. After extensive prompt engineering, the model still occasionally generates malformed JSON. What is the most targeted next step?

text.en: Switch to a larger 70B model via API to solve the formatting issue
Fine-tune the model on a curated dataset of (instruction, valid JSON output) pairs
Re-train the model from scratch on your domain data
Accept the malformed outputs and post-process them with regex

explanation.en: When prompt engineering cannot reliably enforce a specific output format, supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, correct-format output) pairs is the targeted and cost-effective solution. It teaches the model the exact schema adherence required. Re-training from scratch is extremely expensive and unnecessary. A larger model helps general capability but not necessarily strict format adherence, and regex post-processing is brittle.

question.en: Which quantization format is most commonly used for running LLMs efficiently on CPU or low-VRAM GPU environments with llama.cpp?

text.en: GPTQ
AWQ
GGUF
BF16

explanation.en: GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) is the standard format used by llama.cpp and compatible runtimes like Ollama and LM Studio. body.en:
Instruction tuning aligns a pretrained language model to follow user instructions using supervised fine tuning on instruction response examples. A good dataset maximizes signal while minimizing noise and leakage.

Schema design: Each example should contain fields that the target model and training code expect. Common fields include id, system (policy or persona), instruction (user goal), optional input or context, response (assistant ground truth), and metadata such as source, license, language, difficulty, topic, safety flags, and quality rating. For chat style SFT, store a messages array with role labeled turns (system, user, assistant) and optional tool calls and tool results so that turn taking is explicit.

Formatting: Use a deterministic chat template compatible with the model family. This typically includes role tags, separators, and end of turn markers. Apply the same template for every example to avoid spurious variation. For single turn formats, use prompt completion pairs with clear separators between instruction, optional context, and the expected answer. Ensure all samples end with the model specific end of sequence token during training.

Quality controls: Remove duplicates and near duplicates using hashing and approximate matching (n gram overlap, MinHash, or embedding similarity). Normalize whitespace and punctuation, standardize code blocks and markdown, and strip system artifacts. Redact or filter PII and unsafe content according to your deployment policy. Prefer verified or high confidence answers; avoid synthetic hallucinations unless validated. Keep refusal examples and safety demonstrations labeled so the model learns safe behavior.

Length and constraints: Respect context window limits. Truncate or segment long inputs while keeping full target responses when possible. Balance tasks, domains, and difficulty so the model does not overfit narrow patterns. Include multilingual signals only if the target model and tokenizer support them, and tag language explicitly.

Licensing and provenance: Track dataset source and license for each record. Avoid training on content whose terms prohibit redistribution or derivative ML use. Store dataset and preprocessing code versions for reproducibility.

Tool use and function calls: When supervising tool use, include structured turns that capture the assistant decision to call a tool, the tool input, the tool output, and the final user facing response. Keep these elements in the same example so the training loss covers the rationale and the result.

• Record schema: instruction, optional context, response, system, and rich metadata
• Chat formatting: consistent role tokens and end of turn markers matched to the target model template
• Quality gates: deduplication, normalization, safety and PII filtering, and license tracking

• Use a role aware schema and deterministic template aligned with the target model
• Enforce rigorous deduplication, normalization, safety, and licensing checks
• Preserve supervision signal by keeping outputs complete and managing input length
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to design, format, and quality control datasets for instruction tuning.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to choose appropriate random, stratified, group, and temporal split strategies 2) How to prevent data leakage with global deduplication and grouping 3) How to build reproducible splits and obtain reliable performance estimates

Goals of splitting: Train uses most data for fitting the model, validation guides model selection and early stopping, and test provides a final unbiased estimate. Good splits preserve distribution while preventing leakage of information.

Strategies: Random splits are simple but can leak signals when correlated samples exist. Stratified splits maintain class or attribute proportions (task type, language, difficulty). Group aware splits keep all examples sharing a group identifier (user, repository, document, conversation thread, problem family) in the same split to avoid leakage. Temporal splits respect time order for time evolving data (train on past, validate on recent, test on future) to better reflect deployment.

Leakage prevention: Perform global deduplication before splitting using exact hashing and approximate methods (n gram Jaccard with MinHash or SimHash, or embedding similarity with LSH). Blocklist evaluation items from training. For code tasks, split by repository or problem id. For QA over documents, split by document or source. For multi turn chats, keep entire threads intact within one split.

Sizing and balance: Typical ratios are 80 10 10 or 90 5 5 for large datasets, but use more validation if heavy hyperparameter search is expected. Ensure stratification across key attributes so validation and test reflect deployment. For small datasets, use k fold cross validation or repeated stratified splits and report mean and variance.

Reproducibility: Fix random seeds, log the split script and dataset version, and persist the list of ids per split. Verify splits by measuring overlap and near duplicate rates between splits. Document the rationale (e.g., temporal, group aware) and any deviations from overall distribution.

Monitoring shift: Compare label distributions, lengths, topics, and languages across splits. Large discrepancies indicate potential bias and unstable evaluation.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to design and run a reproducible baseline evaluation for an open-source LLM.
- 2) How to choose representative datasets and task-appropriate metrics (e.g., accuracy/EM for QA, F1 for NER, pass@k for code).

A strong baseline quantifies what your starting model can do before you change weights, ensuring any post–fine-tuning gains are real and attributable. Select evaluation sets that reflect how the model will be used: public benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag) for general ability and in-domain dev/test sets for product tasks.

Define clear, task-appropriate metrics: exact match or accuracy for short-form QA/math, F1 for classification/NER, ROUGE/BLEU or model-based similarity for summarization, and pass@k for code generation. Use an evaluation harness (e.g., EleutherAI lm-eval-harness or a custom script) to standardize prompts, stop criteria, and metrics.

Control confounders by fixing the prompt template, context and few-shot examples, decoding (temperature=0, consistent max_new_tokens), and random seeds; prefer deterministic decoding for baselines. Report uncertainty via multiple shards, bootstrap confidence intervals, or paired tests (e.g., McNemar) when comparing models.

Log everything needed for reproducibility: model and tokenizer versions/commits, evaluation code hash, datasets and their versions, prompts, decoding parameters, and hardware. Perform error analysis by clustering failures (reasoning, factuality, formatting) to inform data collection and fine-tuning targets.

Be aware of potential pretraining contamination on public benchmarks; document this risk and complement with private, leakage-checked evals.

title.en: Bias, leakage and data quality checks

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to identify and measure dataset and model bias across subpopulations.
- 2) How to detect and prevent data leakage (train–test overlap, label leakage, and prompt/template leakage).
- 3) How to run scalable data quality checks (deduplication, overlap scanning, label error detection, language/PII filters) and document governance.

Bias refers to systematic performance or content differences across groups (e.g., gender, race, locale) and can manifest as stereotyping, toxicity disparities, or unequal error rates. Measure bias with subgroup metrics (e.g., accuracy gaps, toxicity rate differences) and controlled prompting so groups see comparable contexts; report uncertainty and practical significance.

Leakage occurs when information from the target leaks into training or evaluation: label leakage (answers embedded in inputs), split leakage (duplicates/near-duplicates across train/dev/test), or prompt/template leakage (including ground-truth fields in the prompt). Prevent leakage with careful templating, rigorous split strategies (by source/user/time), and overlap scanning.

In this lesson you will learn:
• The definition and mechanics of full fine-tuning for large language models

Full fine-tuning updates every parameter of a pre-trained model on a downstream dataset. While this yields maximum flexibility and often the highest task-specific accuracy, it requires GPU memory proportional to the full model size plus optimizer states, which can exceed hundreds of gigabytes for modern LLMs. Storage also becomes costly because a separate model copy is saved per task.

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) addresses these constraints by freezing the majority of pre-trained weights and introducing a small set of trainable parameters. Techniques such as LoRA, prefix tuning, and adapter layers fall under this umbrella. PEFT methods typically train fewer than 1% of total parameters, slashing memory and compute requirements dramatically while retaining most of the performance of full fine-tuning. This makes them the practical default for practitioners working with limited hardware or needing to maintain multiple task-specific adapters on a single base model.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) hypothesizes that the weight updates needed during fine-tuning lie in a low-dimensional subspace. Instead of updating a weight matrix W directly, LoRA freezes W and adds two small matrices A and B such that the effective update is ΔW = B × A, where the rank r of these matrices is much smaller than the original dimensions. Only A and B are trained, reducing trainable parameters dramatically.

QLoRA (Quantized LoRA) combines LoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat quantization (NF4) of the frozen base model weights, introduced by Dettmers et al. in 2023. The base model is loaded in 4-bit precision with double quantization to further compress memory, while LoRA adapters are computed in 16-bit. This allows fine-tuning of 65B-parameter models on a single 48 GB GPU — previously impossible. Implementation relies on the bitsandbytes library for quantization and the PEFT library for LoRA configuration. Key parameters include rank r (typically 4–64), lora_alpha (scaling factor), lora_dropout, and target_modules specifying which linear layers receive adapters.

TRL (developed by Hugging Face) is a library for training language models with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and supervised fine-tuning. Its SFTTrainer class is a specialized wrapper around the standard Hugging Face Trainer that streamlines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of LLMs on instruction or conversational datasets.

SFTTrainer accepts a model (or model name), a tokenizer, a training dataset, an optional PEFT config (e.g., LoraConfig), and an SFTConfig object that replaces TrainingArguments. Key SFTConfig parameters include max_seq_length for context window control and packing, which concatenates short examples into full-length sequences for GPU efficiency. SFTTrainer also integrates natively with bitsandbytes for QLoRA workflows. Once configured, training is launched with trainer.train(), and the resulting adapter is saved via trainer.save_model(). This high-level API abstracts away boilerplate, letting practitioners focus on data quality and hyperparameter decisions.

title.en: Hyperparameters and What Can Go Wrong

body.en:
The most critical fine-tuning hyperparameters are learning rate, batch size (via gradient accumulation), number of epochs, LoRA rank, and warmup steps. Learning rates for LLM fine-tuning typically range from 1e-5 to 5e-4; too high causes loss spikes and divergence, too low yields slow or incomplete convergence. After fine-tuning with PEFT, your adapter weights are a small delta on top of the frozen base model. Saving them with model.save_pretrained() writes only the adapter config and weights, typically a few hundred megabytes instead of tens of gigabytes. You can push directly to the Hub with push_to_hub().

When you need a self-contained model—for inference servers that do not support PEFT, or for export to ONNX or GGUF—you merge the adapter back into the base weights using merge_and_unload(). This call folds the low-rank matrices into the original weight tensors, returning a standard HuggingFace model with no adapter overhead. Always save the merged model separately; the original base model and adapter should be retained for reproducibility. Quantized adapters (QLoRA) must be dequantized before merging to avoid precision loss in the fused weights.

A model card is a structured document published alongside a model repository that communicates what the model does, how it was trained, its known limitations, and how it should—and should not—be used. It is the primary artifact that enables other practitioners, auditors, and regulators to assess fitness for purpose.

The Hugging Face model card spec uses YAML front matter for machine-readable fields such as language, license, datasets, metrics, and base_model. The prose sections cover model description, intended uses, out-of-scope uses, biases, training data, training procedure, evaluation results, and a carbon footprint estimate. Dataset cards follow a parallel structure focusing on data sources, collection methodology, preprocessing steps, known quality issues, and the license governing redistribution. The ModelCard class in huggingface_hub lets you create, validate, and push cards programmatically, ensuring metadata stays consistent with the repository contents.

Managing a fine-tuned LLM in production involves ongoing cost control, governance accountability, and a disciplined lifecycle process. Fine-tuning costs are dominated by GPU compute: track hours, instance type, and cloud region using experiment tracking tags so each adapter checkpoint has an associated cost record. Serving costs scale with tokens per second and concurrency; use autoscaling and spot or preemptible instances where latency SLAs allow.

Governance requires maintaining an audit trail from training data through deployment, including data licenses, bias evaluations, and sign-off records. Implement role-based access controls on model repositories and restrict who can promote a model to production. Define a lifecycle policy: models enter staging after evaluation, graduate to production after approval, and are deprecated with a sunset date when a better version is ready. Monitor production traffic for distribution shift using embedding-space drift detectors or output quality proxies, and feed alerts into automated retraining triggers. Versioning adapters and merged checkpoints with semantic version tags makes rollback straightforward when regressions are detected.

question.en: Which serving cost optimization strategy is most appropriate when a workload can tolerate occasional interruptions and has no strict latency SLA?

text.en: Using on-demand dedicated GPU instances reserved for three years
Running inference exclusively on CPU to avoid GPU costs entirely
Deploying on spot or preemptible GPU instances to reduce cost significantly
Disabling continuous batching to reduce power consumption

explanation.en: Spot or preemptible instances are offered by cloud providers at 60-90% discounts in exchange for the possibility of interruption. Batch or async workloads with flexible SLAs are ideal candidates, making this a common cost optimization for LLM serving.

question.en: What is the purpose of a staging-to-production promotion gate in a model lifecycle policy?

text.en: It automatically compresses the model weights before deployment to production
It ensures evaluation metrics, bias audits, and stakeholder approvals are all satisfied before live traffic exposure
It converts the model to ONNX format to meet production performance requirements
It merges all pending adapter checkpoints into a single release candidate

explanation.en: A promotion gate is a formal review step that requires quantitative evaluation benchmarks, bias and safety assessments, and human sign-offs to all pass before a model version is deployed to production, reducing the risk of regressions or harmful outputs reaching users.

question.en: Which technique is used to detect when a deployed model is receiving inputs that differ significantly from its training distribution?

text.en: Adapter merging
Continuous batching
Distribution shift monitoring using embedding-space drift detectors
YAML front matter validation

explanation.en: Distribution shift monitoring compares statistical properties of live inputs or outputs—often using embedding-space distance metrics or output quality proxies—against a reference baseline to detect when the model is being asked to handle data outside its validated distribution, signaling a need for retraining.
